faqs.question: How do you set up a Halloween treasure hunt for kids?
faqs.answer: Pick the trail that fits your youngest reader, write 5 or 6 clue cards, and hide each card at the spot the previous clue names. Hide the treasure last, keep card 1 in your hand, and walk the route once before the children start.

faqs.question: How many clues should a kids' treasure hunt have?
faqs.answer: Five clues suits most children aged 4 to 12, and the three trails on this page use 4 or 5 per version. Under-4s lose a chained trail after about 2 cards, so give them a one-room search instead.

faqs.question: What are good Halloween treasure hunt clues for 5-year-olds?
faqs.answer: Picture clues: draw the next hiding spot and print 3 to 6 sight words under it, such as LOOK UNDER THE MAT. Kindergartners are expected to read common high-frequency words by sight, so keep every other word out.

faqs.question: How do I make treasure hunt clues harder for 10 to 12 year olds?
faqs.answer: Swap words for codes. Backwards writing, a line with every vowel removed, a three-letter shift and a first-letters sentence each take a few minutes to crack, and a hand-drawn map with a red cross makes a good final card.

faqs.question: Where should you not hide treasure hunt clues?
faqs.answer: Never in or on an oven, microwave, fridge, freezer, washing machine, dryer or dishwasher, and never on high shelves, dresser tops or TV stands. Children under 6 accounted for 69.9% of US emergency visits for furniture and TV tip-overs from 1990 to 2019.

faqs.question: How many adults do I need for a kids' treasure hunt?
faqs.answer: Our working ratio is 1 adult per 4 children aged 4 to 6, 1 per 6 aged 7 to 9 and 1 per 8 aged 10 to 12. Add one more adult for any garden trail so somebody stays with the treasure.

faqs.question: What can I use as treasure instead of candy?
faqs.answer: A card decoder wheel, a small torch for each child and a ticket to pick the Halloween film all outlast the night. If you include food, keep it sealed with the label on and check with every parent first.

faqs.question: Can I run a Halloween treasure hunt in a small flat?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each indoor trail uses everyday spots such as a towel rail, a dining chair, a pillow, a tissue box or a rug, and the picture trail fits on one floor.

faqs.question: How long does a Halloween treasure hunt take?
faqs.answer: Our estimates are 10 to 15 minutes of play for the picture trail, 15 to 20 for the rhyming trail and 20 to 30 for the cipher trail. Set-up takes 15 to 25 minutes once the cards are written.

faqs.question: Can a treasure hunt end with a digital Halloween card?
faqs.answer: Yes, for one child. The last clue can point to a tablet showing a Halloween page in Kids tone, and the premium page can be password-locked with the answer to the final cipher card.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Treasure Hunt for Kids: 3 Clue Trails by Reading Age

A Halloween treasure hunt for kids is a trail of 5 or 6 clues in which each card names the next hiding spot and the last leads to one treasure. Match the clue to the reader: pictures for ages 4 to 6, rhymes for 7 to 9 and codes for 10 to 12. All three trails are below, each with an indoor and a garden version. If the treasure ends on a screen, plan for it: 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, and 38.5% of creators lock their page with a password, which the cipher trail can hand over as its final answer. Safe hiding spots, adult numbers and allergy-safe treasure follow.

## What is a Halloween treasure hunt?

A Halloween treasure hunt is a chained clue game: children solve one clue, find the card it points to, and continue until they reach one hidden prize. The order is fixed and there is one finish line.

The model is older than Halloween parties. In Robert Louis Stevenson's [*Treasure Island* (1883) on Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/120), the map carries three red-ink crosses, the note "Bulk of treasure here" and bearings such as "Tall tree, Spy-glass shoulder". Trail 3 borrows that map.

## Which clue type suits which reading age?

Write each clue at the youngest player's solo reading level. The US [Common Core standards for reading foundational skills](https://www.thecorestandards.org/ELA-Literacy/RF/) expect kindergartners to recognise rhyming words and read common words by sight (the, of, to, you, my, is), second graders to decode regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels, and third graders to decode multisyllable words.

So ages 4 to 6 get a drawing plus 3 to 6 sight words; ages 7 to 9 get a two-line rhyme of short words; ages 10 to 12 get a code, because reading is no longer the hard part. In UK terms, kindergarten is Year 1 and grade 3 is Year 4.

Let children ask rather than rescuing them. In a [preregistered 2025 *npj Science of Learning* experiment](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12770468) with 103 children aged 5 to 7, those encouraged to ask questions in eight science lessons valued new information more than those told to listen, and children with less background knowledge gained most. Tell players before card 1 that any question is welcome, and answer with a nudge, never the spot.

## 3 Halloween treasure hunt clue trails, indoor and outdoor

Every clue below is original to this page; the bracket names where that card sends players. For a printable layout, rule one A4 or US Letter sheet into 6 boxes, one clue per box, number each box, and cut. Put the garden version on a different-coloured sheet so the sets never mix.

### 1. Picture trail for ages 4 to 6: 5 clues

Draw the spot, print the words in capitals underneath, and read them aloud the first time. Keep to one floor.

- **Card 1, draw a doormat:** "LOOK UNDER THE MAT." *(front doormat)*
- **Card 2, draw a box of toys:** "GO TO THE TOY BOX." *(toy box)*
- **Card 3, draw a book with a bat on it:** "FIND MY BAT BOOK." *(lowest bookshelf)*
- **Card 4, draw a curtain with two eyes:** "WHO IS IN THE CURTAIN?" *(hem of a floor-length curtain)*
- **Card 5, draw a table with a blanket over it:** "GO IN THE CAVE. BOO!" *(blanket den under the table: treasure)*

For the garden, use the sandpit lid, the biggest tree trunk and the swing seat, with the treasure in a basket on the back step. Every spot should be visible from where one adult stands.

### 2. Rhyming trail for ages 7 to 9: 5 clues

Hand over the first card; the rest wait at the bracketed spots. Nearly every word has one or two syllables, which suits a grade 2 or 3 reader.

- "Bath time's done, I dry you off, then hang upon my rail; unfold me and you'll find the next clue on this spooky trail." *(folded bath towel)*
- "Four legs, no feet, I stand all day where people sit to eat; crouch down low and look beneath my flat and wooden seat." *(dining chair, card taped under the seat)*
- "Left and right, in pairs we wait with laces, straps and soles; check the rack where shoes all rest, a clue hides in the holes." *(shoe rack)*
- "Every night your head lies here, so soft and plump and white; slip a hand inside my case, the clue is tucked in tight." *(pillow)*
- "Long and comfy, three can sit and gaze out at the night; creep round behind my back to find the treasure, out of sight!" *(behind the sofa: treasure)*

The garden version runs 4 clues:

- "Pegs and pins live in my bag beside the washing line; reach in and feel among the clips, the next clue's there, it's fine." *(peg bag)*
- "A green snake coiled around a wheel, I water every bed; unwind me just a loop or two, your clue is there instead." *(hose reel)*
- "A little man in a pointy hat who never moves or talks; look behind his painted boots, beside the garden walks." *(garden ornament)*
- "Where summer lunches sit outside, I'm wide and flat and tall; crawl below my top to find the treasure, best of all." *(garden table: treasure)*

### 3. Cipher trail for ages 10 to 12: 5 coded clues

Print each code's rule at the foot of its card. Bracketed answers are for adults.

- **Card 1, read it backwards:** "XOB EUSSIT EHT NI KOOL" *(Look in the tissue box)*
- **Card 2, every vowel removed:** "LFT TH FRT BWL" *(Lift the fruit bowl)*
- **Card 3, move each letter 3 back, so D becomes A:** "RSHQ WKH DWODV" *(Open the atlas)*
- **Card 4, first letters only:** "Ravens Usually Gossip." *(the rug, card slid flat under one corner)*
- **Card 5, the map:** a sketch of the room with one red cross and a Stevenson-style note, "Rug corner, bearing to the window, four steps." *(treasure under the cross)*

In the garden, use "HCNEB EHT REDNU KOOL" (look under the bench), "VKDNH WKH SHJ EDJ" (shake the peg bag) and "Toads Always Paddle." (the outside tap). Finish with a garden map.

## Halloween treasure hunt trails compared

The trails side by side, plus mixed ages. Times and adult ratios are our working estimates, not an official standard.

| Trail | Ages | Clues (indoor / garden) | Reading it needs | Set-up and play (est.) | Adults |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picture | 4–6 | 5 / 5 | Sight words, kindergarten | 15 min; 10–15 min | 1 per 4 children |
| Rhyming | 7–9 | 5 / 4 | Two-syllable words, grades 2–3 | 20 min; 15–20 min | 1 per 6 children |
| Cipher | 10–12 | 5 / 5 | Multisyllable words, grade 3 up | 25 min; 20–30 min | 1 per 8 children |
| Mixed 4–12 | All | Picture and cipher at once | Each child at own level | 40 min; 20–30 min | 2 or more |

Pick by the youngest reader in each team. Add one adult for any garden trail.

## Where never to hide a clue, and how many adults you need

Never put a card in or on an oven, microwave, fridge, freezer, washing machine, tumble dryer or dishwasher. A child who learns that clues live inside machines may open one later without you.

Skip high shelves, the tops of dressers and TV stands, and any spot reached by standing on a chair. [Lu and colleagues' 2021 *Injury Epidemiology* study](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8394564) estimated 560,203 US children were treated in emergency departments for furniture or TV tip-overs from 1990 to 2019, about 18,673 a year. Children under 6 made up 69.9% of them, and in that age group 19.5% of injuries came from pulling furniture onto themselves and 11.3% from climbing it.

Outdoors, avoid ponds, water butts, tool sheds, bins and the street side of any fence. Within the table's ratios, put one adult where the trail turns a corner and one at the treasure.

## What to put in the treasure chest

One shared treasure, split equally, stops the finish becoming a grab. Paint a shoebox black, mark a red cross on the lid, and fill it with 3 things that outlast 31 October:

- **A card decoder wheel per child:** two card circles with the alphabet round each, joined by a paper fastener, so cipher players can write the next hunt. Keep fasteners from toddlers.
- **A small torch per child:** the next hunt can run in a dark room.
- **A "first pick" ticket:** the finder chooses the film on Halloween night, Saturday 31 October 2026 or Sunday 31 October 2027.

Food is optional. If you add any, keep it sealed with the ingredient label on, check with every parent first, and ban swaps.

## End the hunt with a card for one child

The last clue can point to a tablet instead of a box, for one child: a grandchild in another city, or your own child at bedtime. The [interactive Halloween card with a Kids tone](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes and holds up to six photos; Kids tone means round blushing ghosts, no gore, no jump scares, and a No button that waits as "maybe later?".

For a bigger finale, the [cinematic Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes, holds up to 12 photos, and shows no No button in kids mode. Its optional unlock time shows only their name and a countdown; make the password the answer to the last cipher card. Pages average 11.1 views each, so expect replays.

Both are one-person greeting pages, not party tools. For a birthday hunt near Halloween, the [full template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) covers other occasions.

## When a treasure hunt is the wrong plan

Under-4s lose a chained trail after 2 cards; scatter a few big objects in one room instead. A group bigger than 12 needs two trails starting at different cards, or the first spot becomes a crowd.

A 9-year-old who finds reading hard can take the picture trail without comment. SubhSandesh pages are English-only, need a screen and cannot run a group game, so for a party of ten the paper cards are the tool.

## Sources

- Stevenson, R. L., *Treasure Island*, 1883 (Project Gutenberg eBook 120).
- Common Core State Standards Initiative, Reading: Foundational Skills, Kindergarten to Grade 3, 2010.
- Park et al., *npj Science of Learning*, 16 December 2025.
- Lu et al., *Injury Epidemiology*, 27 August 2021.
- SubhSandesh platform data, measured 24 September 2026.
